newsitem.title: USA: New York mayor, legal groups challenge U.S. laws.
newsitem.headline: New York mayor, legal groups challenge U.S. laws.

text.p: New York's Republican mayor, in an alliance with liberal legal groups, sued the federal government on Wednesday over provisions in the new immigration and welfare laws that cut assistance to the poor.

New York City and several public-interest groups charged in separate lawsuits in U.S. District Court in Manhattan that taking food stamps and cash benefits from the elderly and disabled who are legal residents but not citizens violated the Constitution.

"Legal residents pay taxes and contribute on an equal basis with everyone else and now unfortunately the federal government is saying that although they're willing to take their money on an equal basis, when they have difficulty the federal government is walking away from them," Mayor Rudolph Giuliani told a news conference, with representatives of advocacy groups at his side.

Giuliani, who has cast himself as a national spokesman on immigration, also sued the federal government last October challenging the constitutionality of provisions in the new welfare and immigration laws that allow city employees to turn in undocumented immigrants who seek public services such as police protection, hospital care and education.

The welfare law signed by President Bill Clinton last August bars most immigrants admitted legally to the United States from receiving food stamps and Supplemental Security Income benefits for the elderly and disabled poor. Clinton has since asked Congress to restore about $14 billion in aid to legal residents.
Legal groups filed lawsuits on Wednesday on behalf of about 100,000 legal immigrants in New York, Vermont and Connecticut who face elimination from food stamps and SSI disability aid.
Congressional Republicans who crafted the welfare law have argued that non-U.S. citizens should not be entitled to federal benefits. The United States accepts an estimated 700,000 immigrants a year.
Taking a position that sets him aside from many in his own party, the mayor of immigrant-dominated New York City has given speeches in Boston, Minneapolis and Washington in recent months.
